subject: chemistry
unit_name: Classification of Elements and Periodicity in Properties
overview: This unit explains how elements are arranged in the modern periodic table on the basis of atomic number and electronic configuration. It then uses that arrangement to explain periodic trends in atomic and ionic size, ionization enthalpy, electron gain enthalpy, valence and chemical reactivity. NEET asks 2-3 direct questions every year from this unit, mostly ordering of trends, exceptions and assertion-reason items on electronic configuration, so it is high-scoring with focused revision.

topics.explanation: The modern periodic law, based on Moseley's work, states that the physical and chemical properties of elements are periodic functions of their atomic numbers. The present long form of the table has 7 horizontal periods and 18 vertical groups, numbered 1 to 18 as recommended by IUPAC. The period number equals the principal quantum number $n$ of the outermost shell. The number of elements in a period is twice the number of atomic orbitals filled during that period (e.g. 3s + 3p, 4 orbitals, gives 8 elements in period 3), giving 2, 8, 8, 18, 18, 32 and 32 elements in periods 1 to 7. Elements in the same group have similar outer electronic configurations and hence similar properties. The 14 lanthanoids (Ce to Lu) and 14 actinoids (Th to Lr) are placed separately at the bottom to keep the table compact. Elements with $Z > 100$ are given temporary IUPAC names built from numerical roots, for example $Z = 101$ is unnilunium (Unu).
key_points: Basis of the modern table is atomic number, not atomic mass
7 periods and 18 groups; period number equals $n$ of the valence shell
Period lengths are 2, 8, 8, 18, 18, 32 and 32
Period 6 starts with the filling of 6s and period 7 with 7s
Lanthanoids (4f) belong to period 6 and actinoids (5f) to period 7
IUPAC roots: nil 0, un 1, bi 2, tri 3, quad 4, pent 5, hex 6, sept 7, oct 8, enn 9; the name ends in -ium
Examples of temporary names: 104 is unnilquadium (Unq) and 120 is unbinilium (Ubn)

formulas.meaning: Locates the period of an element from its electronic configuration
Moseley's relation between X-ray frequency and atomic number; it is the basis of the modern periodic law

topics.neet_tip: Expect questions on the IUPAC name or symbol of elements with $Z > 100$, and on locating the period or group of an element from its atomic number.
topics.topic: Modern periodic law and present form of the periodic table

topics.explanation:
Elements are divided into four blocks according to the orbital that receives the last (differentiating) electron.

The s-block (groups 1 and 2, configuration $ns^{1-2}$) contains reactive metals with low ionization enthalpy.

The p-block (groups 13 to 18, configuration $ns^2np^{1-6}$) contains metals, non-metals and metalloids. Together with the s-block, these are the representative or main group elements.

The d-block (groups 3 to 12, configuration $(n-1)d^{1-10}ns^{0-2}$) contains the transition metals. They show variable oxidation states, coloured ions and paramagnetism. Zn, Cd and Hg ($d^{10}$) are not typical transition elements.

The f-block (configuration $(n-2)f^{1-14}(n-1)d^{0-1}ns^2$) contains the inner transition elements, the lanthanoids and actinoids. Elements after U are called transuranium elements.

Helium ($1s^2$) is an s-block element by configuration but is placed in group 18 because of its noble gas properties. Hydrogen is placed separately in many tables because it resembles both alkali metals and halogens.
key_points: Block is decided by the orbital receiving the last electron
s-block: groups 1 and 2, configuration $ns^{1-2}$
p-block: groups 13 to 18, configuration $ns^2np^{1-6}$
d-block: groups 3 to 12, configuration $(n-1)d^{1-10}ns^{0-2}$
f-block: configuration $(n-2)f^{1-14}(n-1)d^{0-1}ns^2$
Metalloids: B, Si, Ge, As, Sb, Te
Metallic character decreases across a period and increases down a group
He is placed in group 18 although its configuration is $1s^2$

formulas.meaning: Gives the group for s-block elements

topics.explanation:
Atomic radius is expressed in three ways:

Covalent radius is half the internuclear distance in a covalent molecule.
Metallic radius is half the internuclear distance between neighbouring atoms in a metal lattice.
Van der Waals radius is half the distance between non-bonded atoms; it is the largest of the three.

Across a period, atomic radius decreases because the effective nuclear charge increases while electrons enter the same shell. Down a group, radius increases because new shells are added, and this outweighs the increase in nuclear charge. Noble gases appear largest in their periods because only van der Waals radii can be measured for them.

A cation is smaller than its parent atom because it has fewer electrons attracted by the same nuclear charge. An anion is larger than its parent atom because the added electrons increase repulsion and lower the effective nuclear charge per electron. In an isoelectronic series, the species with the higher nuclear charge is smaller.

Two anomalies follow from poor shielding by d and f electrons. Ga (135 pm) is slightly smaller than Al (143 pm) because of poor shielding by 3d electrons. The lanthanoid contraction makes Zr and Hf almost equal in size.
key_points: Size order of radius types: van der Waals > metallic > covalent
Radius decreases across a period and increases down a group
Cation < parent atom < anion
Isoelectronic order: $N^{3-} > O^{2-} > F^- > Na^+ > Mg^{2+} > Al^{3+}$
For ions of the same element, higher positive charge means smaller size: $Fe^{3+} < Fe^{2+}$
Ga is slightly smaller than Al because 3d electrons shield poorly
Zr and Hf have nearly equal radii because of the lanthanoid contraction
Shielding power of orbitals: $s > p > d > f$

formulas.meaning: Effective nuclear charge, where $\sigma$ is the shielding constant; higher $Z_{\text{eff}}$ gives a smaller radius
Covalent radius from the bond length of a homonuclear molecule
Quick rule for ordering isoelectronic ions by size

topics.neet_tip: The most frequent question is arranging isoelectronic ions, or a cation, its atom and an anion, in increasing or decreasing order of size.
topics.topic: Periodic trends: atomic and ionic radii

topics.explanation:
Ionization enthalpy ($\Delta_iH$) is the energy required to remove the most loosely bound electron from an isolated gaseous atom in its ground state. Successive ionization enthalpies always increase ($\Delta_iH_2 > \Delta_iH_1$) because the electron is removed from an increasingly positive ion.

Across a period, ionization enthalpy generally increases because $Z_{\text{eff}}$ increases and the atom becomes smaller. Down a group, it decreases because size and shielding increase.

Two types of exceptions occur:

Be > B and Mg > Al. In B and Al, a 2p or 3p electron is removed. A p electron penetrates less towards the nucleus and is better shielded than an s electron, so it is easier to remove.

N > O and P > S. N has a stable, symmetrical half-filled $2p^3$ configuration. In O ($2p^4$), two electrons occupy the same 2p orbital, and the resulting electron-electron repulsion makes one of them easier to remove.

Noble gases have the highest values in their periods, and He has the highest first ionization enthalpy of all elements. A very large jump between successive ionization enthalpies shows that a noble gas core is being broken.
key_points: Ionization is always endothermic; $\Delta_iH$ is positive
Successive values increase: $\Delta_iH_1 < \Delta_iH_2 < \Delta_iH_3$
Period 2 order: $Li < B < Be < C < O < N < F < Ne$
Period 3 order: $Na < Al < Mg < Si < S < P < Cl < Ar$
He has the highest first ionization enthalpy; Cs is lowest among stable elements
Na: first value 496 kJ $mol^{-1}$ and second value 4562 kJ $mol^{-1}$, a huge jump
Penetration of orbitals towards the nucleus: $s > p > d > f$
Low ionization enthalpy means strong metallic and reducing character

formulas.meaning: Defines the second ionization enthalpy, which is always larger
Reference value for the hydrogen atom

topics.neet_tip: NEET tests ordering of first ionization enthalpies with the Be/B and N/O exceptions, often as assertion-reason items that ask whether the stated reason truly explains the trend.

topics.explanation:
Electron gain enthalpy ($\Delta_{eg}H$) is the enthalpy change when an electron is added to an isolated gaseous atom to form an anion. For most elements it is negative, meaning energy is released.

Across a period, it becomes more negative because $Z_{\text{eff}}$ increases and size decreases. Down a group, it generally becomes less negative because size increases. Halogens have the most negative values because adding one electron gives them a noble gas configuration.

Some elements have positive values:
Noble gases, because the electron must enter a new, higher shell.
Be and Mg, because their s subshell is filled.
N, which is nearly zero or slightly positive because of its stable half-filled $2p^3$ configuration.

An important exception occurs in the second period. The added electron enters the small, compact $n = 2$ shell and faces strong electron-electron repulsion. As a result, F is less negative than Cl, and O is less negative than S.

Second electron gain enthalpies are always positive. For example, $O^- \rightarrow O^{2-}$ requires energy because of repulsion from the negative ion.
key_points: Most negative electron gain enthalpy of all elements belongs to Cl, about $-349$ kJ $mol^{-1}$
Magnitude order for halogens: $Cl > F > Br > I$
Magnitude order for group 16: $S > Se > Te > O$; O is about $-141$ and S about $-200$ kJ $mol^{-1}$
Noble gases, Be, Mg and N have positive or near-zero values
Second electron gain enthalpy is always positive
Electron affinity is sometimes quoted with the opposite sign to $\Delta_{eg}H$
Second period elements show smaller magnitudes because of their small, compact shells

formulas.meaning: Shows that second electron gain enthalpy is positive

topics.neet_tip: The halogen order $Cl > F > Br > I$ (by magnitude) and the O versus S comparison are asked repeatedly in single-correct questions.

topics.explanation:
Valence of representative elements equals either the number of valence electrons or eight minus the number of valence electrons. Oxidation state is the charge an atom appears to carry in a compound, assigned on the basis of electronegativity.

In $OF_2$, oxygen shows +2 because F is more electronegative and always shows −1. In $Na_2O$, oxygen shows −2.

The periodic table lets you predict formulas of compounds:
Oxides across period 3: $Na_2O$, $MgO$, $Al_2O_3$, $SiO_2$, $P_4O_{10}$, $SO_3$, $Cl_2O_7$, where the group oxidation state reaches its maximum.
Hydrides across period 3: $NaH$, $MgH_2$, $AlH_3$, $SiH_4$, $PH_3$, $H_2S$, $HCl$.

In heavier p-block elements, the inert pair effect makes the oxidation state two units below the group valence more stable. Examples are Tl(+1), Pb(+2) and Bi(+3).

Transition and actinoid elements show variable oxidation states because both $(n-1)d$ and $ns$ electrons, or f electrons, can take part in bonding.

First members of groups show anomalous behaviour. Their maximum covalency is 4 because only 2s and 2p orbitals are available. For example, B forms $[BF_4]^-$, whereas Al forms $[AlF_6]^{3-}$. Second period elements also show diagonal relationships with the element diagonally below them: Li-Mg, Be-Al and B-Si.
key_points: Valence for groups 1, 2, 13 and 14 equals the number of valence electrons
Valence for groups 15, 16 and 17 is usually 8 minus the number of valence electrons
F always shows −1 oxidation state; O shows +2 in $OF_2$
Maximum oxidation state usually equals the group valence, as in $Cl_2O_7$ (+7) and $SO_3$ (+6)
Inert pair effect stabilises Tl(+1), Pb(+2) and Bi(+3)
Second period elements have maximum covalency 4 (no d orbitals); B forms $[BF_4]^-$ but Al forms $[AlF_6]^{3-}$
Diagonal pairs: Li-Mg, Be-Al, B-Si
Use the group of an unknown element to predict its oxide or hydride formula

formulas.meaning: Common valence of groups 15 to 17 towards H or metals
Predicts the highest oxidation state of most p-block elements; F (maximum −1, or 0 in $F_2$) and O (maximum +2, in $OF_2$) are exceptions

topics.neet_tip: NEET asks you to predict the formula of a compound formed between two elements given by their atomic numbers or groups, or to identify the inert pair effect.

topics.explanation:
Chemical reactivity depends on ionization enthalpy, electron gain enthalpy and electronegativity. Electronegativity is the tendency of a bonded atom to attract the shared electron pair; on the Pauling scale F is highest (4.0), followed by O (3.5).

Reactivity is highest at the two extremes of a period:
On the left, alkali metals have very low ionization enthalpy, lose electrons easily and are strong reducing agents.
On the right, halogens have highly negative electron gain enthalpy and high electronegativity, gain electrons easily and are strong oxidising agents.
Reactivity is lowest in the centre of the period and among the noble gases.

Metallic character, basic nature of oxides and reducing power decrease across a period. Non-metallic character, acidic nature of oxides and oxidising power increase across a period.

Across period 3, oxides change from strongly basic $Na_2O$, through amphoteric $Al_2O_3$, to strongly acidic $Cl_2O_7$. Down a group, metallic character increases.

In aqueous solution Li is the strongest reducing agent ($E^\circ = -3.04$ V) because of its very high hydration enthalpy, although its ionization enthalpy is the highest in group 1. Among the halogens, $F_2$ is the strongest oxidising agent.
key_points: Metallic and reducing character are highest at the lower left of the table
Non-metallic and oxidising character are highest at the upper right
F is the most electronegative element; electronegativity increases across a period and decreases down a group
Oxide nature across period 3: $Na_2O$ (basic), $Al_2O_3$ (amphoteric), $SiO_2$, $P_4O_{10}$, $SO_3$, $Cl_2O_7$ (increasingly acidic)
Other amphoteric oxides: $BeO$, $ZnO$, $SnO$, $PbO$
Li is the strongest reducing agent in water because of its high hydration enthalpy
$F_2$ is the strongest oxidising agent
Basic oxide plus water gives a base, e.g. $Na_2O + H_2O \rightarrow 2NaOH$; acidic oxide plus water gives an acid, e.g. $Cl_2O_7 + H_2O \rightarrow 2HClO_4$

formulas.meaning: A basic oxide forms a base in water
An acidic oxide forms an acid in water
An amphoteric oxide reacts with both acid and base

topics.neet_tip: Questions focus on the acidic, basic or amphoteric nature of oxides and on the reducing or oxidising power of elements at the extremes of a period.

common_traps: Assuming F has the most negative electron gain enthalpy. Cl does, because the added electron in F's small 2p shell faces strong electron-electron repulsion.
Expecting first ionization enthalpy to rise smoothly across a period. Be > B and N > O (and Mg > Al, P > S) are exceptions; for O the cause is repulsion between the paired 2p electrons.
Thinking noble gases are the smallest atoms of their period. Their van der Waals radii are compared with the covalent radii of other elements, so they appear the largest.
Believing Ga is larger than Al. Ga is slightly smaller because its 3d electrons shield poorly.
Calling Li the weakest reducing agent of group 1 because it has the highest ionization enthalpy. In water it is the strongest because of its very high hydration enthalpy.
Taking the second electron gain enthalpy of O as negative. It is positive, since an electron must be added to an already negative ion.
Placing He in the s-block of the periodic table. Despite its $1s^2$ configuration, it sits in group 18.
Ordering isoelectronic ions by mass number or charge sign alone. The ion with the higher nuclear charge is always smaller.
quick_revision: Modern periodic law: properties are a periodic function of atomic number; the table has 7 periods and 18 groups.
Period lengths are 2, 8, 8, 18, 18, 32 and 32; the period number is $n$ of the valence shell.
Atomic radius decreases across a period and increases down a group; cation < atom < anion.
Isoelectronic species: higher Z gives smaller size, e.g. $Al^{3+}$ is the smallest of $N^{3-}$ to $Al^{3+}$.
Ionization enthalpy increases across a period and decreases down a group; He is highest and Cs lowest.
Ionization enthalpy exceptions: Be > B and Mg > Al (s versus p electron); N > O and P > S (half-filled versus paired p electrons).
Electron gain enthalpy: Cl is the most negative; noble gases, Be, Mg and N are positive or near zero; second values are always positive.
Electronegativity: F is the highest (4.0); it increases across a period and decreases down a group.
Maximum oxidation state equals the group valence for most elements, as in $Cl_2O_7$ (F and O are exceptions); the inert pair effect gives Tl(+1) and Pb(+2).
Oxides change from basic ($Na_2O$) to amphoteric ($Al_2O_3$) to acidic ($Cl_2O_7$) across period 3.
Second period elements have maximum covalency 4 and show diagonal relationships Li-Mg, Be-Al and B-Si.
